core: working definition of inventory: goods held for sale in the normal course of business, plus goods in production for that sale and the materials that go into them
the three types: raw materials, work in progress, finished goods
inventory as an asset until sold (balance-sheet placement)
counting and valuing inventory: physical counts, FIFO, LIFO, weighted average
the costs of inventory: holding costs, obsolescence, tied-up cash
inventory and the income statement: sold goods become cost of goods sold
honest framing: inventory is money sitting on shelves, neither too much nor too little
supporting: goods available for sale = beginning inventory + purchases
GAAP versus IFRS treatment of cost-flow methods (LIFO not permitted under IFRS)

the supply-chain inventory view (owned by introduction-to-business)

tax rules around LIFO and inventory methods (no tax advice)

claims.claim: Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds to sell to customers in the normal course of its operations; the international standard IAS 2 defines inventories as assets held for sale in the ordinary course of business, and US GAAP describes the same idea (goods the company means to sell).

Manufacturers hold three types of inventory: raw materials (inputs before work begins), work in progress (partially completed units), and finished goods (complete and ready for sale); a merchandiser's inventory is equivalent to finished goods.
Unsold inventory is an asset reported on the balance sheet; when goods are sold their cost is reported as cost of goods sold, an expense on the income statement.

Goods available for sale equals beginning inventory plus purchases during the period; sold goods become cost of goods sold and remaining goods become ending inventory, so the two always add back to goods available for sale.

The main cost-flow methods are FIFO (earliest purchases assumed sold first), LIFO (latest purchases assumed sold first), and weighted average (total cost divided by total units), plus specific identification for unique items; US GAAP permits them, while IFRS permits specific identification, FIFO, and weighted average but not LIFO.
Carrying inventory costs money: holding costs (storage, insurance, handling), the risk of obsolescence, and cash tied up in goods that have not yet sold.
Inventory records drift from reality through shrinkage — spoilage, theft, damage, or miscounting — which physical counts reveal.
For many companies inventory is a significant portion of current assets; OpenStax reports that in 2018 Walmart's inventory was roughly 70 percent of current assets and 21 percent of total assets.
Periodic inventory systems determine inventory values at the end of each period, while perpetual systems update values after every transaction; inventory is often the least liquid current asset.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether LIFO is an acceptable cost-flow method.
positions: US GAAP permits LIFO; OpenStax notes the AICPA estimates roughly 35-40 percent of US companies use it.
IFRS does not permit LIFO; IAS 2 lists specific identification, FIFO, and weighted average as the cost formulas.
CFI notes some methods may be prohibited in certain countries under certain accounting standards.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names FIFO, LIFO, and weighted average with one-line factual mechanics, and notes in a single sentence that IFRS does not permit LIFO. It offers no tax advice and takes no position on which method is better.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether cost-flow methods describe the physical movement of goods.
positions: OpenStax PoA 10.1: a company's cost allocation is based on estimates of cost flow and is unrelated to the actual flow of the physical inventory.
Everyday usage of 'first-in, first-out' often refers to physically rotating stock (e.g., perishables).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents FIFO, LIFO, and weighted average strictly as costing assumptions and flags the physical-flow confusion in Common Mistakes.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Accounting, Volume 1: Financial Accounting, Section 10.1: Describe and Demonstrate the Basic Inventory Valuation Methods and Their Cost Flow Assumptions
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Read live via HTTP with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (openstax.org serves the full page content in the initial HTML). Supports: inventory as a company asset of goods available for sale; raw-materials / work-in-process / finished-goods process levels for manufacturers, with a merchandiser's inventory equivalent to finished goods; unsold inventory reported as an asset on the balance sheet and sold goods as cost of goods sold on the income statement; goods available for sale = beginning inventory + purchases; the four costing methods (specific identification, FIFO, LIFO, weighted average) with one-line mechanics; weighted-average computation (total cost divided by total units); shrinkage (spoilage, theft, damage); the IFRS Connection note that IFRS does not permit LIFO while US GAAP does; Walmart 2018 inventory at roughly 70% of current assets and 21% of total assets. Facts restated in original prose; used reference-only because the OpenStax footer restricts AI ingestion.

sourceRecords.title: What Is Inventory? Raw Materials, WIP, & Finished Goods
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (record reused from the phase-2 source registry, identical URL). Supports: inventory as a current asset on the balance sheet consisting of all raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods a company has accumulated; finished goods as complete and ready for immediate sale; work-in-progress as partially completed units in production; raw materials as inputs on which work has not yet begun; ending inventory = beginning balance + purchases - cost of goods sold; the four calculation methods (FIFO, LIFO, weighted average, specific identification); periodic systems valuing at period end versus perpetual systems after every transaction; inventory as often the most illiquid current asset. Page states no explicit license, so REFERENCE_ONLY; facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, 10.4 Pulling It Together: Resource Planning
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (record reused from the phase-2 source registry, identical URL). Supports: inventory as the supply of goods held for use in production or for sale to customers; the inventory trade-off (large inventories meet production and customer demand and earn quantity discounts, but tie up money, cost to store, and can become obsolete); the goal of keeping down holding costs while maintaining enough on hand. Only the definition and trade-off framing were used here; the supply-chain management view belongs to the introduction-to-business subject. Concepts adapted into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: IAS 2 Inventories
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (standards body). Read live via HTTP and cross-checked against an Internet Archive capture on 2026-08-21. Supports: IAS 2 as the international standard for determining the cost of inventories and the subsequent recognition of the cost as an expense; inventories measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value; cost assigned by specific identification for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and by the first-in, first-out or weighted-average cost formula for interchangeable items; when inventories are sold, their carrying amount is recognized as an expense; the standard's use of 'ordinary course of business' in describing selling price. Standard text is copyrighted; used reference-only, no wording reproduced.
